data.chapter: Late Medieval Conflict and the Wars of the Roses
data.sourceTitle: Why the Wars of the Roses Began
data.targetTitle: Why the Wars of the Roses Began
data.sourcePassage:
The Wars of the Roses were not caused by one simple event. They grew from long-term, medium-term and short-term causes that built up over several decades.

Both Lancaster and York were branches of the royal family, both tracing descent from King Edward III. Henry VI, the Lancastrian king, was personally gentle and devout, but many nobles believed he lacked the strength needed for medieval kingship. He was expected to lead armies, reward loyal followers, punish disorder and control noble rivalries. He struggled with all of these. When Henry suffered a serious period of mental illness in 1453, nobles competed to control the government in his absence.

England's loss of most of its French lands by 1453 added to the political pressure. Defeat damaged Henry VI's reputation. Some nobles had lost lands and income connected to France. Soldiers and politicians blamed each other. This created resentment that made factional politics even more dangerous.

Factions were groups of nobles who worked together for political power. If one faction controlled the king, rivals feared they would be excluded, punished or ruined. Richard Duke of York presented himself as a reformer who wanted to remove corrupt advisers. Over time, his challenge became more directly a claim to the throne. The First Battle of St Albans in 1455 — when armed forces loyal to York and Lancaster clashed and Henry VI was captured — showed that political rivalry had become armed conflict.

questions.question: What was expected of a medieval king according to the passage?
options: To remain neutral in all noble disputes and avoid conflict
To lead armies, reward loyal followers, punish disorder and control noble rivalries
To hold regular elections to choose government advisers
To leave all decisions to Parliament
questions.modelAnswer: A medieval king was expected to lead armies, reward loyal followers, punish disorder and control noble rivalries. Henry VI struggled to meet these expectations.

questions.question: How did England's loss of French lands in 1453 contribute to the Wars of the Roses?
options: It gave Lancaster and York equal French territories to fight over
It directly gave Henry VI a stronger claim to the throne
It damaged Henry VI's reputation and created resentment among nobles who had lost lands and income
It had no effect on the political situation in England
questions.modelAnswer: Defeat in France damaged Henry VI's reputation as a ruler. Nobles who had lost lands or income in France blamed poor royal leadership, creating resentment that intensified factional politics.

questions.question: What did the First Battle of St Albans in 1455 demonstrate?
options: That Henry VI had successfully defeated all Yorkist opposition
That political rivalry between noble factions had escalated into armed conflict
That Lancaster and York had agreed to share power peacefully
That ordinary people had started the fighting independently of the nobles
questions.modelAnswer: The First Battle of St Albans showed that the political rivalry between Lancastrian and Yorkist factions had become armed conflict, with Henry VI captured by Yorkist forces.

questions.question: The passage identifies long-term, medium-term and short-term causes. What is the value of this approach to explaining historical events?
options: It proves that all events have exactly three causes
It shows that complex events usually result from multiple factors building up over time, rather than one single trigger
It shows that only short-term causes matter in history
It proves that the Wars of the Roses were inevitable from the moment Henry VI was born
questions.modelAnswer: Identifying long-term, medium-term and short-term causes shows that complex events like civil wars are usually the result of multiple factors accumulating over time. No single cause is sufficient on its own.

data.chapter: Late Medieval Conflict and the Wars of the Roses
data.section: Noble Power and the Course of Conflict
data.sourceTitle: Noble Power, Private Armies and Changing Kings
data.targetTitle: Noble Power, Private Armies and Changing Kings
data.sourcePassage:
Late medieval nobles were very powerful. A great noble might control large estates, castles and networks of retainers — people who served him in return for wages, protection and legal help. When nobles used retainers to form private armies, royal authority was weakened. Private armies could intimidate local communities, threaten rivals and make political disputes violent.

Edward Duke of York, son of Richard Duke of York, became King Edward IV after his victory at the Battle of Towton in 1461. Towton was one of the bloodiest battles fought on English soil. It replaced the Lancastrian Henry VI with a Yorkist king. However, the conflict continued. The Earl of Warwick, once Edward's key supporter, turned against him. In 1470, Henry VI was briefly restored to the throne before Edward returned in 1471, defeating his enemies at Barnet and Tewkesbury. Henry VI's son was killed at Tewkesbury, and Henry VI himself died in the Tower of London.

Edward IV ruled more securely until his death in 1483. His brother Richard Duke of Gloucester was appointed Protector for the young Edward V. Instead of governing for his nephew, Richard declared Edward V and his brother illegitimate, and took the throne as Richard III. Edward V and his brother Richard — the Princes in the Tower — were last known to be in the Tower of London in 1483. They then disappeared. Their fate remains one of history's most debated mysteries.

Richard III was not the only person who might have gained from the princes' deaths. However, he had the means and the motive. Historians argue because the evidence is limited, biased and often written after the events under Tudor rule.

questions.question: What was a retainer?
options: A legal adviser who worked for the king
A person who served a noble in return for wages, protection and other support
An official who collected taxes for the government
A monk who kept records for the Church
questions.modelAnswer: A retainer served a noble in return for wages, protection, land or legal help. Nobles built up retinues that could act as private armed forces.

questions.question: Why was Towton a significant turning point?
options: It was the last battle of the Wars of the Roses
It replaced the Lancastrian Henry VI with the Yorkist Edward IV
It ended noble power in England permanently
It was where Henry Tudor defeated Richard III
questions.modelAnswer: Towton replaced the Lancastrian Henry VI with the Yorkist Edward IV, making it a major turning point. It was one of the largest battles fought on English soil.

questions.question: What happened to the Princes in the Tower?
options: They escaped to France and continued to challenge Richard III
They were executed publicly to deter future Lancastrian challenges
They disappeared from the Tower and their fate remains a historical mystery
They survived and later became kings of England
questions.modelAnswer: The Princes in the Tower disappeared from public view in 1483 while held in the Tower of London. Their fate remains a historical mystery because the evidence is limited and biased.

questions.question: The passage says historians 'argue because the evidence is limited, biased and often written after events under Tudor rule'. What does this mean for studying the Princes in the Tower?
options: We should accept the Tudor version of events as the most accurate
Because key evidence is biased by Tudor writers, historians must weigh sources carefully and acknowledge uncertainty
It proves that Richard III definitely ordered the murder of the princes
It means no historical judgement at all can be made about the princes
questions.modelAnswer: Because the main sources were written under Tudor rule by people who may have had reasons to criticise Richard III, historians cannot take them at face value. They must weigh the evidence carefully and acknowledge genuine uncertainty.

data.chapter: Late Medieval Conflict and the Wars of the Roses
data.sourceTitle: Henry VII, Tudor Legitimacy and Propaganda
data.targetTitle: Henry VII, Tudor Legitimacy and Propaganda
data.sourcePassage:
Henry Tudor had a Lancastrian claim to the throne but it was not especially strong. He had spent years in exile. He gained support from those who opposed Richard III, and at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485 his forces defeated Richard. A key factor was the Stanley family, who waited before choosing sides. When they backed Henry at the decisive moment, Richard was defeated and killed.

Henry VII understood that winning a battle was not enough. He needed people to accept that his rule was legitimate. He dated his reign from the day before Bosworth, which meant those who had fought for Richard could legally be accused of treason. He was crowned king and secured Parliament's recognition. In 1486 he married Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV, uniting the Lancastrian and Yorkist claims. The Tudor rose — combining red and white — became a symbol of this union.

Henry VII also used propaganda to strengthen his position. Tudor writers and later Shakespeare's famous play presented Richard III as physically deformed, scheming and murderous. These images were politically useful for the Tudors. However, historians must treat them carefully. Most sources about Richard were written after his defeat, by people who lived under Tudor rule and who could benefit from presenting him negatively.

Bosworth was a turning point that ended the Wars of the Roses. However, Henry VII still faced Yorkist challenges, including the pretender Lambert Simnel and the Battle of Stoke Field in 1487. The Tudor dynasty brought greater stability over time, but establishing that stability required law, marriage, military victory and careful control of how the past was remembered.

questions.question: Why did Henry VII marry Elizabeth of York?
options: To end the war with France
To unite the Lancastrian and Yorkist claims and strengthen his legitimacy
Because Elizabeth was a close friend from childhood
To prevent a Scottish invasion
questions.modelAnswer: Henry VII married Elizabeth of York to unite the Lancastrian and Yorkist claims. This strengthened the Tudor dynasty's legitimacy by suggesting it represented both rival houses.

questions.question: Why did Henry VII date his reign from the day before Bosworth?
options: Because it was his birthday and he wanted to celebrate
So that those who had fought for Richard III could be legally accused of treason against the king
Because Parliament required all kings to start their reigns a day early
To show that he was older and more experienced than Richard III
questions.modelAnswer: By dating his reign from the day before Bosworth, Henry VII made it technically treason to have fought for Richard III on the day of battle. This allowed him to punish opponents legally.

questions.question: Why should historians be careful about sources that portray Richard III negatively?
options: Because all history is false and nothing can be trusted
Because most such sources were written after his defeat by people living under Tudor rule who could benefit from criticising him
Because Richard III was actually a popular and successful king
Because Shakespeare's play is a primary source written during Richard III's own lifetime
questions.modelAnswer: Most sources portraying Richard III negatively were written after his defeat by people living under Tudor rule. These writers may have had political reasons to present Richard badly, making their evidence potentially biased.

questions.question: The passage says Henry VII used 'law, marriage, military victory and careful control of how the past was remembered'. What does this suggest about how rulers maintain power?
options: Military victory alone is sufficient to maintain power long-term
Rulers need multiple tools — legal, symbolic, military and narrative — to build lasting authority
Only marriage can secure a dynasty's long-term survival
Once a ruler wins a battle, their power is automatically secure
questions.modelAnswer: Henry VII used several different tools: legal measures against opponents, marriage to strengthen claims, military victories and propaganda shaping memory. This suggests that lasting power requires more than just winning battles — it needs legitimacy, narrative and institutional support.
